plain7.alt: Three versions against three checks on the CPU-DRAM design. Older version, our pinned 6.0 build: 0.01 degrees off the paper, passing the 1 degree bar set in advance; heat out exceeds heat in by 1.39 percent, failing the balance check; 6.3 degrees from three separate solvers. Newer version 7.0: 117 degrees off the paper, failing; heat balances within rounding; 102 degrees from the solvers. Newer version with one step changed, as Delfie reports and ScienceClaw reports too: 9.6 degrees off the paper, failing; heat balances within rounding, as ScienceClaw reports; 3.3 degrees from the solvers. Saved 45 mm, grid 64 CPU-DRAM cases, simulated, not compared with a real chip. The heat check's rounding limit is about 0.43 watts, 0.063 percent, and is not a total error bound. Each column uses its own reading. The paper column uses the native all-block reading, 232.67 degrees for 7.0. The solver column uses the hottest chiplet entry, 224.67 degrees for 7.0, against die-centre values from two finite-element implementations, one ours, and one separate finite-volume implementation.

slides.title: Of course I know everything about chip design.
slides.caption: Chiplets: small chips on one base. They get hot.
slides.footer: Simulated heat map of a published reference design. Simulated, not silicon.
slides.say: I'm a computer engineer. I took a chip-design class. Of course I know everything about chip design. I do not know anything about chip design. All I know is a chip package is a few small chips, chiplets, that get hot, and you can't put them too close together or too far apart. But I'll tell you what: my agents know chip design.
slides.cue: Pause after "everything about chip design." Then, deadpan: "I do not know anything about chip design." Let the last line land. Before the talk: one real timed rehearsal with the actual demo.

slides.title: What agents need, and only what they are allowed to touch.
slides.footer: Staging output, 08:39 UTC, 1 November: our own team's test runs with our stage client, not outside arrivals.
slides.say: I'm building Senti. It recognizes agents, sets them up, lets them collaborate, serves what they need, and keeps a record of what they did. Delegation is scoped; drift and rogue agents are handled gracefully, because each only gets what it's allowed to touch. Shopping, security, and today, science.

slides.title: In the model: the link from lid to cooler.
slides.line: Two other teams reported results from changing that link.
slides.footer: Delfie (delphisci team) and ScienceClaw reported results from changing that modeled link; those reports are separate from our verified reference reproduction. Simulated, not silicon.
slides.say: They localized a difference around the modeled link between the metal lid and cooler. Then they started discussing spreader-to-sink coupling. Which sounds like a plumbing emergency, but apparently it can ruin your experiment. Two other teams reported results from changing that link.

slides.title: Passing one check isn't passing them all.
slides.label: simulated, not silicon
slides.footer: Delfie (delphisci team) reports the one-step change; ScienceClaw reports reproducing it and computed its heat balance. The figure carries each column's own reading and limits.
slides.say: Our fixed reference test with the older setup reproduced two published values within a hundredth of a degree. But in a saved CPU-DRAM case, 1.39 percent more heat left the model than entered. The modified output is reported within rounding and nearer the separate solvers; it still misses the paper. Source analysis found non-reciprocal lateral links consistent with that. I nodded.

slides.footer: Every temperature in this talk is simulated, not measured on silicon.
slides.say: That's the point: the simulator grades the agent. Check the grader before celebrating the score.
slides.heading: Check the grader before celebrating the score.

finalFallback.footer: Within six minutes of our ask, two other teams reported reruns in their own setups. Both reported the same direction.

slides.say: My ambition? Make you wonder why your agents need Kiro, Jira, Slack, Facebook, and GitHub. Okay, not GitHub. Yet. Give Senti a try, man. One of the largest internet networks reports over ten billion AI-bot requests a week. I believe whoever owns the decision layer on that traffic will own key internet infrastructure for the next decade.
slides.cue: "Okay, not GitHub. Yet." is the quiet aside. Naming the network out loud is Carter's call (aneta recommends naming it); the slide stays neutral.

backup.title: Other solvers: descriptive, not a verdict.
items: Two finite-element implementations and a separate finite-volume implementation report about 78 and 122 degrees for these two designs. Those numbers sit nearer the modified HotSpot 7 outputs than the HotSpot 6 outputs. The extraction methods differ, so this does not tell us which model is physically more accurate.
What is compared: die-centre readings from those implementations against HotSpot's selector values.
Whose: one finite-element implementation is ours; the other is an outside team's, and the finite-volume implementation is another outside team's, unnamed until it consents.
Differences, descriptive only: about 0.7 and 3.3 degrees from the modified 7.0, and about 2.6 and 6.3 degrees from 6.0.
